ACTIONS TIMEOUT-MINUTES CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Which of your Actions jobs can hang for six hours?

A GitHub-hosted job with no timeout-minutes is cancelled only after GitHub's default of 360 minutes. One deadlocked test or stalled download then holds a runner — and on a private repository, bills minutes — for six hours instead of a few. Paste your workflow YAML below and this page lists every job that has no timeout, or one set to the 360 default, with the worst-case billed minutes for its runner and the one-line fix.

Nothing is uploaded. The YAML you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own.

1. Paste one or more workflow files

Copy the contents of each file under .github/workflows/ you want checked. Add more blocks for more files — nothing here reads your repository, so pasting is how it sees anything.

Paste at least one workflow file above and click Check.

Findings

File : LineTypeDetailFix

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                  # scan .github/workflows under the current directory
python3 check.py /path/to/repo    # scan a specific checkout
python3 check.py --format json    # machine-readable
python3 check.py --fail-on-risk   # exit 2 if any finding exists

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Wire --fail-on-risk into your own CI to block a job added without a timeout before it merges.

Common questions

What happens to a GitHub Actions job with no timeout-minutes?

A job on a GitHub-hosted runner that never sets timeout-minutes is cancelled only when it reaches GitHub's default limit of 360 minutes (six hours). A deadlocked test, a stalled download or a step waiting on input then holds the runner — and, on a private repository, bills minutes — for the whole six hours.

Why does the runner type change the number?

On private repositories GitHub's documented minute multipliers are higher for Windows and macOS runners than for Linux, so the same hung six hours consumes more of your included minutes. Check GitHub's current billing page for the live multipliers; this tool uses them only to print an upper bound.

Is timeout-minutes: 360 a real limit?

No. 360 is the default restated, so it limits nothing. This tool flags it separately because it looks like a guard when it is not.

Does this tool fetch anything from GitHub for me?

No. It makes no network calls at all — nothing here can, because nothing here talks to a server. Paste your workflow YAML and the scan runs entirely in this page.

Does a clean scan mean my workflows are safe?

No. This checks one specific pattern in a single workflow file at a time. It is not a security audit or a cost audit, and it does not choose a correct timeout for you — too short a timeout cancels healthy runs. It does not look at step-level timeouts or at the called workflow behind a reusable-workflow call.

More: what is timeout-minutes and what should you set it to?

what-is-github-actions-timeout-minutes.h.text:
← Actions timeout-minutes Check

GitHub Actions timeout-minutes: the default, the cost, and what to set

Every job in a workflow can carry a timeout-minutes value. Leave it out and GitHub applies its default: the job is cancelled after 360 minutes, six hours.

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - run: npm test

What is the default timeout for a GitHub Actions job?

A job on a GitHub-hosted runner is cancelled after 360 minutes (six hours) unless timeout-minutes sets a lower limit. A hung job therefore holds the runner, and on a private repository bills minutes, for up to six hours.

Why the default hurts

Most CI jobs take minutes. When one hangs — a deadlocked test, a dependency download that stalls, a command waiting for input that never comes — nothing stops it until minute 360. The runner is held the whole time, and on a private repository every one of those minutes is metered against your plan. GitHub documents higher minute multipliers for Windows and macOS runners than for Linux, so the same hang costs more there; check GitHub's current billing page for the live numbers.

A value of 360 is not a guard

Writing timeout-minutes: 360 restates the default. It looks like a limit and limits nothing, which is why the checker flags it separately.

Choosing a value

  • Look at how long the job normally takes in your run history, then set the limit at a few times that. A test job that takes 4 minutes can carry 15.
  • Too tight a limit cancels healthy runs when the runner is slow, so leave headroom rather than aiming at the average.
  • Put it on the job, not on a step. A step-level timeout-minutes bounds that one step only.
  • A job that calls a reusable workflow (uses:) cannot take timeout-minutes; set it on the jobs inside the called workflow.

Check your own workflows

Paste your workflow YAML into Actions timeout-minutes Check to find every job without a job-level limit across all your workflow files at once, or run the CLI in your own repository:

python3 check.py --fail-on-risk

That exits with a nonzero status if any job has no timeout or restates the default — wire it into your own CI to block a new one before it merges.

No warranty. This page and the tool it describes are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. This is not a security audit or a cost audit, and a clean scan does not mean a workflow is safe or cheap — only that this one pattern was not found. Minute figures are upper bounds, not predictions.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. Free, experimental, may move or go offline without notice.

Everything on the linked tool runs in your browser; nothing you paste is uploaded, and the tool makes no network calls of its own.
